title: Use `Stream.iterate` with a predicate (Java 9) to generate numbers from 1 to 100: `Stream.iterate(1, n -> n <= 100, n -> n + 1)`.
shortTitle: Use Stream.iterate with a predicate (Java 9) to generate numbers from 1 to 100

s1_definition.profdef: The three-argument `Stream.iterate(seed, hasNext, next)` (Java 9) adds a predicate that terminates the stream when it returns false. `Stream.iterate(1, n -> n <= 100, n -> n + 1)` produces one through one hundred and stops on its own — no `limit` needed.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya counts up from one, adding one each time, and stops automatically the moment the number would exceed one hundred.
s1_definition.oneliner: Three-arg `iterate(seed, hasNext, next)` is a functional for-loop that self-terminates — no `limit` required.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The three-argument `Stream.iterate(seed, hasNext, next)` (Java 9) adds a predicate that terminates the stream when it returns false. `Stream.iterate(1, n -> n <= 100, n -> n + 1)` produces one through one hundred and stops on its own — no `limit` needed.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya counts up from one, adding one each time, and stops automatically the moment the number would exceed one hundred.

**One line to remember:** Three-arg `iterate(seed, hasNext, next)` is a functional for-loop that self-terminates — no `limit` required.

sections.s2_technical:
The Java 9 overload `Stream.iterate(seed, hasNext, next)` takes a start value, a predicate that decides whether to continue, and a function for the next value. `Stream.iterate(1, n -> n <= 100, n -> n + 1)` starts at one, continues while n is at most one hundred, and increments by one, so it generates exactly one through one hundred and terminates itself.

This is the functional equivalent of a classic for-loop: seed is the initialiser, the predicate is the loop condition, and the next function is the increment. Unlike the two-argument iterate, it needs no limit because the predicate bounds it.

The senior nuance is that this overload makes bounded sequences self-terminating and far clearer than two-argument iterate plus limit, especially when the bound is a value condition rather than a count. It reads like a for-loop expressed as a stream. I still prefer `IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 100)` for a simple contiguous int range because it is even clearer and primitive, reserving three-argument iterate for non-trivial step functions or non-contiguous sequences.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A utility at the National Bank of India generates a bounded sequence with a custom step and a value-based stop condition, such as installment numbers up to a limit.

This is exactly what three-argument iterate does — it self-terminates on the predicate without a separate limit.

The code defines a `SequenceService.oneToHundred method and a demo.
sections.s5_journey:
Step 1: iterate seeds at one.

Step 2: Before each element, the predicate checks whether n is at most one hundred.

Step 3: While true, the next function adds one, producing one, two, three, up to one hundred.

Step 4: When n would become one hundred one, the predicate returns false and the stream terminates on its own.

```
INFO: count=100 first=1 last=100
```

```

    │ seed=1 → check n<=100 → emit → n+1 → ...
    │ stops when n would exceed 100 (self-terminating)
    ▼
  [1, 2, 3, ..., 100]   (no limit needed)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The three-argument Stream dot iterate added in Java 9 takes a seed, a predicate that decides whether to continue, and a next function. iterate of one, n at most one hundred, n plus one starts at one, continues while the value is at most one hundred, and increments by one, so it generates exactly one through one hundred and terminates itself — no limit is needed. It reads like a classic for-loop expressed as a stream, where the seed is the initialiser, the predicate is the loop condition, and the next function is the increment.

The improvement over the two-argument iterate is that the predicate bounds the stream, so I do not have to tack on a limit, and it is especially clear when the stop condition is a value test rather than a simple count. At the National Bank of India I use it for bounded sequences with a custom step and a value-based stop.

The senior point I stress is choosing the right tool. For a plain contiguous integer range I still prefer IntStream dot rangeClosed, because it is even clearer and works on primitives without boxing. I reserve the three-argument iterate for sequences with a non-trivial step function or a non-contiguous progression, where expressing the initialiser, condition, and step as a self-terminating stream is the most readable option.
